title: Why Gold Rises When the World Is Scared (It Pays $0)
description:
Why does gold often rise in a crisis, even though it pays no interest? It is nobody's debt, so it can't default, and many investors and central banks treat it as a safe haven. Central banks bought a net 321 tonnes in Q3 2026, up 42% from a year earlier, and gold averaged $4,262 an ounce, about 23% higher than a year earlier, but about 13% below its Q1 2026 average. Real interest rates (rates after inflation) matter too: gold pays nothing, so higher real rates make it less attractive.

Source: World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends Q3 2026 and press release (Nov 3, 2026); prices are quarterly averages of the LBMA (PM) gold price. Past prices don't predict future ones. This is education, not a recommendation to buy or sell gold. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: Why? Gold is nobody's debt, so it can't default, and can't be printed.
So when the world gets scared, money often runs to it.
Central banks bought a net three hundred and twenty-one tonnes in one quarter.
But here's the catch: safe doesn't mean steady.
From July to September, it averaged about thirteen percent less than January to March.
When rates after inflation rise, gold often struggles. It pays nothing, remember.
The lesson: a safe haven isn't the same as risk-free.
